The file preserves her application as filed, a small record of an ordinary inventor seeking protection for a household tool.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Lawyers_Lawyers: nsia-Lawyers Lawyers: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Smears_Smears:
Morton Mintz reported for the Washington Post on July 12, 1973, under the headline 'Weicker Says He Reported.' Senator Lowell P. Weicker Jr. of Connecticut had reported certain charges to investigators. The charges were attributed to unidentified 'Nixon reelection sources.' Weicker sat on the Senate's Watergate committee, where he had become one of the president's Republican critics.

Anonymous sourcing inside a scandal is itself a story: who is planting charges, and who carries them to the record. Mintz, the Post's careful investigative reporter, lays out what Weicker said he had done with the claims. The article preserves a senator's account of rumor handled through channels, at the summer's height, when the committee's hearings were remaking the scandal daily.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WeisbergFBIReco: The FBI released a set of cross-reference pages from its central records system under the Freedom of Information Act. The pages concern Harold Weisberg, the assassination researcher who sued the government many times for files. Cross-reference pages show how often a name appears across bureau records. For Weisberg, the release is both research material and a record of his long fight to open the files.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
After the Bay of Pigs invasion failed in April 1961, President John F. Kennedy turned on the agency that planned it. This briefing book, posted in April 2026 for the sixty-fifth anniversary, uses newly posted documents on that aftermath. The invasion itself had collapsed within days on a Cuban beach.

Kennedy considered reshaping the CIA and even dismantling it, the documents show. That reaction matters because the failed landing shaped his distrust during the missile crisis a year later. Readers get the paper trail of a president deciding what to do with an intelligence service that had failed him.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_Bom: A Cuban airliner was bombed out of the sky in 1976, killing everyone aboard, in one of the worst terrorist attacks in the hemisphere's history. This briefing-book page revisits that bombing forty years later, drawing on the National Security Archive's records. The evidence here is the title alone, so no specific documents can be named. The page's value is its anniversary framing: the case, and the men long accused of planning it, remained unresolved four decades on.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
In the late 1980s a series of incidents slowly woke the Defense Department to attacks on computer networks. Michael Martelle edited this briefing book, posted in June 2019, twenty years after the response took shape. The military assembled the first joint task force built explicitly around cyber warfare.

That unit, Joint Task Force - Computer Network Defense, was a landmark in organization. Before it, network defense belonged to no one in particular. The records trace how scattered warnings became a standing command with a defined mission, a step every later American cyber unit descends from in some way.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_dnsa_US_:
Jimmy Carter's foreign policy, from 1977 to 1981, is documented here through papers written at the very top. Top-level memos to the president and National Security Council records anchor this publication. Many records were marked eyes only, and some carry Carter's own annotations.

The top secret memos show Carter handling arms control talks and the Iran hostage crisis. They also cover the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in his final year. His working relationships with Secretary of State Cyrus Vance and adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski come through in the paper. The set joined the Archive's award-winning digital series on American foreign policy.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Rum:
Donald Rumsfeld, as secretary of defense, wrote short memos his staff called snowflakes. This posting draws on newly published snowflakes from the war in Afghanistan. Two years after the invasion, they show, Rumsfeld still lacked intelligence on who the enemies were.

That admission from the war's own manager is startling. The United States had toppled the Taliban quickly, then settled into a long fight against an enemy its leaders could not clearly name. A snowflake is a small document, but a run of them records a secretary's frustrations in his own terse style, day after day.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_guatemal: The Guatemala Genocide Ruling, Five Years Later: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
In September 1979 an American Vela satellite recorded a double flash over the South Atlantic, the signature of a nuclear test. William Burr, Avner Cohen, and Richard Wolfson edited this briefing book, number 686, published forty years later in September 2019. Suspicion fell on Israel or South Africa.

A newly posted document shows the CIA saw the probability of a nuclear test as ninety percent or more. Yet White House science advisers dismissed that possibility, and the posting argues their dismissal looks weak against the added evidence. The Vela flash remains officially unexplained. These documents let readers judge the strongest case that a secret test lit up the ocean that night.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_peru_Per:
Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission delivered its final report in 2003, after years of internal conflict with the Shining Path and state forces. On the twentieth anniversary, in August 2023, the Archive posted a core collection of declassified American documents tied to that history.

Evidence here reaches only the anniversary and the collection's existence, so claims stay modest. American documents matter in Peru's reckoning because Washington supported Peruvian governments through the conflict years. A core collection lets readers and researchers test the commission's findings against what United States officials reported at the time. Anniversaries of truth reports are when archives can restart a national conversation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Perestroika was Mikhail Gorbachev's program to rebuild Soviet life in the late 1980s. Thirty years on, the National Security Archive issued Briefing Book number 504 on that effort. Edited by Svetlana Savranskaya and Anna Melyakova and published in March 2015, it gathers newly released records on what reform achieved and where it fell short.

Newly published material includes a report on the Chernobyl disaster and records of Gorbachev's meetings with French leader Francois Mitterrand and President George H. W. Bush. One record holds Gorbachev's 1991 appeal for help from abroad as the Soviet Union came apart. The Archive sums up the record as great gains beside large missed chances, and the papers let readers judge both for themselves.

In December 1988, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev came to New York and met President Ronald Reagan and Vice President George H. W. Bush at Governors Island. Thirty years later, in December 2018, the National Security Archive published declassified documents on that meeting and on the famous United Nations speech Gorbachev gave on the same trip.

In that speech, Gorbachev offered deep cuts in Soviet forces, a move the Archive calls an arms race in reverse. The released papers show the United States and its NATO allies worrying about losing control of the public story of the Cold War. Readers can watch a superpower rivalry turn, in real time, into something closer to partnership, and see how hard that shift was to manage.

George H. W. Bush hosted Mikhail Gorbachev in Washington and at Camp David in the spring of 1990, months after the Berlin Wall fell. Briefing Book number 707, compiled and edited by Thomas Blanton and Svetlana Savranskaya and published in June 2020, presents Soviet and American documents from that summit, thirty years after it happened.

Germany's future dominates the talks, along with the shape of Europe, regional trouble spots, and Moscow's deepening money crisis. Gorbachev leaves with ceremony and a symbolic trade deal, but not the aid or arms cuts he wanted. The papers show a Soviet leader running out of time, and they connect to the editors' award-winning book on the last superpower summits, then due out in paperback.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia_Reading_Barr: When Attorney General William Barr released the Mueller report in 2019, he released it with redactions: black bars hiding grand jury material, ongoing cases, and intelligence methods. A National Security Archive briefing book page takes up the sport of reading those redactions. It studies what the blacked-out text's length, placement, and context reveal. The subject is what Special Counsel Robert Mueller found. His investigation covered Russian election interference and the Trump campaign. Only the page capture is preserved here, marking the Archive's entry in a national pastime of that spring.
podcast-joerogan-Xr0jaqT8eRs:
Jay Anderson joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2430 for a full-length conversation. The entry keeps the show's standard shape: one guest across hours of open talk with Rogan, with the transcript holding the whole session as it aired.

The value of such entries is the record itself, the guest's views and stories in his own words rather than in clips cut by others. Readers can follow the exchange from start to finish and judge the ideas whole. The episode stands in the library as a complete sitting with the day's guest, filed for listeners who want nothing trimmed away.
podcast-joerogan-nMBFf1SIBRs:
Benjamin Franklin is the unlikely star of this Joe Rogan Experience segment about skeletons found in a London basement. Franklin lived in the house for years while serving as a colonial agent. When workers dug into the cellar, they found human bones buried under the floor.

Rogan and his guest sort through why the bones were there. The leading account points to an anatomy school run by Franklin's friend, who used bodies for study and buried the remains in secret. They weigh that sober story against darker rumors. It is a short, strange detour into the hidden side of a founding father.
federalist-papers:
The Federalist Papers are 85 essays written in 1787 and 1788 to win support for the new United States Constitution. Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote them under one pen name, Publius. The essays first ran in New York newspapers during the ratification fight.

The authors explain the Constitution piece by piece and answer the fears of its critics. Famous numbers defend an energetic union, a large republic that tames factions, and the separation of powers. Judges and scholars still cite the papers to read the founders' intent. They stand as the classic work of American political thought.
pindar-odes-myers:
Pindar of Thebes was the greatest lyric poet of ancient Greece. Ernest Myers translated his surviving victory odes into English. The odes celebrate winners at the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games.

Each ode weaves the victor's praise together with myth and moral warning. Pindar warns athletes that glory is brief and pride draws divine anger. His language is dense, soaring, and famously hard to follow. Chariot owners, wrestlers, and boy boxers all receive the same lofty treatment. Myers helps modern readers through the thickets of allusion. These poems defined how Greece praised excellence in public.
jewel-of-seven-stars:
Bram Stoker turned from vampires to the lore of old Egypt in this novel of 1903. He knew the craze for Egypt that filled the press and museums of his age. The tale starts in London, in the calm homes of the rich and learned of Edward's reign.

A queen of old Egypt, Tera, waits in her tomb for a rise back to life. A band of men bring her casket and scrolls to England and plan the rite to wake her. The book is a root text of mummy horror, a kind much copied since its day.
the-haunted-and-the-haunters:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton wrote this tale of a haunted house in 1859. Its full name runs on with the words 'The House and the Brain' as a second title. Bulwer-Lytton was a star of his age, and his ghost tale set the form for all that came next.

A man takes a house in London that no tenant can bear to stay in for one night. He sits up with a friend and a dog to face its dread in a calm, planned way. The tale founds the line of the psychic quest tale, in which men hunt ghosts with method.
northup-twelve-years:
Solomon Northup was a free Black musician and farmer in New York when kidnappers drugged him in 1841. Sold into slavery in Louisiana, he spent twelve years on plantations before friends traced him. His account appeared in 1853, the year of his rescue.

Northup describes cotton and sugar work, overseers, and fellow enslaved people with precise, calm detail. He names places and owners, and court records later backed his story. That makes Twelve Years a Slave the best documented American slave narrative. Its cool tone makes the cruelty it reports hit even harder. A white editor, David Wilson, helped ready the tale for print that year.
grant-personal-memoirs:
Ulysses Grant wrote his Personal Memoirs in 1885 while dying of throat cancer, racing to finish. Mark Twain published the book and championed it. Grant completed it days before his death, and it secured his family's future.

The memoirs cover his West Point years, the Mexican War, and his Civil War commands in plain, clear prose. Shiloh, Vicksburg, Chattanooga, and Appomattox receive his calm, exact judgment. He praises and blames without bitterness, even toward old foes. Critics rank the book among the finest memoirs ever written by a soldier or a president. Twain's firm sold the set door to door with striking success.
addams-twenty-years:
Jane Addams published Twenty Years at Hull-House in 1910, looking back on the settlement house she co-founded in Chicago in 1889. Hull-House stood in a poor immigrant ward on Halsted Street. Addams lived there among her neighbors for decades.

She describes the neighbors who came: Italians, Greeks, Jews, Bohemians, each with old-country ways and new-world troubles. Hull-House offered classes, a nursery, art, and help with jobs and law. Addams also traces her own growth toward labor reform and peace work. The book helped invent American social work and remains its founding memoir.
lee-recollections-letters:
Robert Lee, the youngest son of the Confederate commander, published Recollections and Letters of General Robert Lee in 1904. The book joins his own memories with his father's private letters. It shows Lee the husband and father, not only the general.

Letters to his wife and children reveal Lee's humor, faith, and care for small home affairs. The son recalls camp visits and the family's losses during and after the war. Lee's postwar years at Washington College close the volume. Readers seeking the private voice behind the public legend of duty and defeat will find it here.
dickinson-life-and-letters:
Martha Dickinson Bianchi, Emily Dickinson's niece, published The Life and Letters of Emily Dickinson in 1924. Bianchi had known her aunt and guarded the family papers. Her book mixes biography with letters not printed before.

She describes the Amherst household, the poet's white dress, and her rare meetings with visitors. Family quarrels over the poems' editing hum in the background of the story. The letters show Dickinson's humor and devotion across her whole life. Though later scholars corrected some details, Bianchi's portrait fixed the myth of the recluse poet for a generation of readers. Photographs of the house and family accompany her text in this edition.
stanton-eighty-years:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton published Eighty Years and More in 1898, her reminiscences of a life spent fighting for women's rights. Stanton was the chief philosopher of the American suffrage movement. She looks back from 1815 to 1897, the span in her subtitle.

She recalls her girlhood, the Seneca Falls convention of 1848, and her long partnership with Susan Anthony. Debates over the vote, marriage law, and the church fill the middle years. Her wit is sharp even when her allies fall short of her hopes. The book is both a memoir and a history of the movement she helped found.
catherine-memoirs:
Catherine the Great wrote her memoirs in French over many years, and they surfaced long after her death in 1796. The German princess had come to Russia as a bride and seized the throne from her husband in 1762. Her own account stops before that coup.

She describes the court of the Empress Elizabeth, her loveless marriage to Peter, and her reading of the French thinkers. Intrigue, loneliness, and ambition shape her rise, told in a cool, observant voice. The memoirs break off in 1759, before the seizure of power. Even so, they remain the key source for her early life.
flaubert-sand-letters:
A. L. McKenzie translated the Sand and Flaubert letters in 1921, with Stuart Sherman's opening essay. Sherman notes that the friendship ran twelve years, through the Franco-Prussian War and the Commune. Sand appears in her calm late years at Nohant, ringed by children and grandchildren.

Flaubert, the hermit of Croisset, writes from the opposite pole of life. The two giants argue over art, politics, and how a writer should live. Their exchange is funny, combative, and deeply fond by turns. Sherman calls it rich as biography alone, yet the letters also show two great minds at full stretch for any reader.
brentano-aus-der-chronika-eines-fahrende:
A wandering scholar's chronicle gives Brentano his frame in Aus der Chronika eines fahrenden Schuelers, presented in German. The traveling student moves through a Germany of inns, roads, and chance meetings. Youth and freedom breathe through the fragmentary tale, part picaresque and part meditation.

Episodes gather like entries in a travel diary, warm with the poet's verbal music. The open road itself becomes the hero's teacher, as in so many Romantic daydreams. Melancholy underlies the charm; wandering also means never quite arriving. Brentano left the work in a loose, songlike form that suits its subject. Readers who love the Taugenichts spirit will feel at home here.
raabe-elderflowers:
Fragrant blossoms of early summer give Raabe's novella Elderflowers its name and its mood, in this English translation. Small-town German life again supplies the scene, where ordinary people carry quiet burdens. Dignity and humor, Raabe's twin signatures, mark the way his characters bear them.

Tender, observant, and gently melancholy, the tale shows the author at his most characteristic. Old attachments stir as the elderflowers bloom, and the past leans into the present. Nothing is forced; feeling gathers like scent on warm air. Readers new to Raabe will find a compact sample of his gifts. Those who know him will recognize the beloved hand at once, unhurried and kind.
bandelier-delight-makers:
Adolph Bandelier founded much of Southwestern archaeology in the United States. His novel The Delight Makers first appeared in 1890, here in a 1918 edition. He set the tale among the Pueblo peoples in the age before Spain came.

Bandelier builds daily life from the ruins and records he knew best. Corn fields, clan rites, hunts, and feuds fill the prehistoric village. A young hero moves through custom, duty, and secret plots. Few novels of the ancient Southwest rest on such deep field knowledge. Science wears the dress of story here, with rare skill and care throughout.
woodroffe-garland-of-letters:
Woodroffe's Garland of Letters appeared in 1922 as studies in mantra-shastra. The Tantric science of sacred sound stands at the book's core. Letters and syllables, in this teaching, are far more than signs.

Woodroffe shows how sound becomes form, deity, and world in Tantra. He traces the fifty letters as powers that build all things. Ritual speech, breath, and the body join in one bold scheme. His prose mixes a scholar's rigor with a devotee's real sympathy. Readers gain the clearest English path into the thought behind mantra practice. The garland of its title strings letters like flowers on one thread.
roscoe-twenty-five-years:
Roscoe told his own story in Twenty-five Years in East Africa in 1921. The memoir covers his mission work and research in Uganda. A young missionary grows, across its pages, into a famed scholar.

Travel, danger, and close watching mark his slow path to trust. He shows how a people's respect is earned, not merely claimed. The human tale behind his great Baganda study stands clear here. Readers meet the man inside the classic work of East African studies. Adventure and patient science share the road in his warm, plain telling. The memoir explains the trust that made his great study possible.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modeste-demer: Bishop Modeste Demers was the first bishop of Vancouver Island, carrying the faith to Canada's Pacific frontier in the 1800s. This entry traces his missionary journeys, his diocese, and his legacy. The apostle of British Columbia, whose journeys spanned the Pacific Northwest's missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-music-of-vesp: Vespers, the evening office, has its own musical world of psalm tones, antiphons, and the Magnificat. This entry traces its chant traditions and their history. The day's end, in song: its psalms close the Church's day as they have for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nevers: Nevers, the Burgundian city on the Loire, is forever linked with St. Bernadette, whose body rests incorrupt in its convent. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. The city of the saint of Lourdes: Bernadette's incorrupt body draws pilgrims there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-taci: This biographical entry profiles Nicholas Tacitus Zegers, a Flemish Franciscan exegete of the 1500s, tracing his career, his biblical commentaries, and his scholarship as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's Franciscan gallery, preserved among its records of Flemish exegetes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-non-jurors: The Non-Jurors were the Anglican bishops and clergy who refused the oath to William and Mary in 1689 and were deprived. This entry traces their schism, their liturgy, and their slow extinction. Conscience against the crown: their last bishop died in 1805.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de: This entry profiles the Marian shrine of Notre-Dame des Ardilliers, tracing its pilgrims, its miracles, and its place in French devotional life as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact sketch from the encyclopedia's French gallery, preserved among its records of Marian shrines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-prea: The Order of Preachers are the Dominicans, St. Dominic's hounds of the Lord, founded to preach against heresy. This long entry traces their foundation, their saints and scholars, and their worldwide work. Eight centuries of the black and white: their schools shaped Catholic thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pamiers: Pamiers, the Ariège town of the Pyrenean foothills, has been a bishop's see since the 1200s. This entry covers its diocese, its bishops, and its history. The faith in the land of the Cathars: its bishops fought the Albigensian heresy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parochial-reg: Parochial registers are the parish books recording baptisms, marriages, and burials. This entry explains their history, their law, and their value to genealogists. The memory of the parish, in ink: the Council of Trent ordered every parish to keep them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrician-bro: The Patrician Brothers were founded by Bishop Delany of Kildare in 1808 to teach Ireland's poor boys. This entry traces their foundation, their schools, and their spread. The teaching brothers of Ireland: their humble schools spread to India and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-melchers: Cardinal Paul Melchers led Cologne's Catholics through Bismarck's Kulturkampf, suffering exile for the faith. This entry traces his archiepiscopate, his trials, and his courage. The confessor of the Kulturkampf: his patient exile witness shamed the proud new German empire utterly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulist-fathe: The Paulist Fathers were founded by Isaac Hecker in 1858 to convert America. This entry traces their foundation, their missions, and their spirit. The missionaries to the Americans: their street missions preached boldly to Protestants and to lapsed Catholics alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penitential-o: Penitential orders were the congregations devoted to penance and the conversion of sinners. This entry surveys their foundations, their rules, and their work. The orders of the sackcloth: their stern penance converted many hardened public sinners of medieval Europe too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-donders: Blessed Peter Donders was the Redemptorist who spent his life among Surinam's lepers and slaves. This entry traces his mission, his charity, and his beatification. The apostle of the lepers: his lonely Batavia mission never rested or complained of its hardships.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-poit: Peter of Poitiers was the Paris theologian whose Sentences taught the twelfth century. This entry covers his career, his works, and his school. The chancellor of the schools: his lucid Sentences once outshone even the great Lombard's at old Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poitiers: Poitiers, the city of the great battle and the baptismal font of St. Martin, became a diocese. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The Church in the city of Charles Martel: its ancient baptistery is the oldest in France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presentation-: The Presentation Brothers are Edmund Rice's teaching congregation. This entry traces their foundation, their schools, and their spirit. The brothers of the poor scholar: their humble schools dot Catholic Ireland's towns and cities still today in living faith and charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-queen-s-daugh: The Queen's Daughters are the society of Catholic women under Mary's patronage. This entry notes their foundation, their works, and their spirit. The daughters of the heavenly Queen: their devout sodalities serve the urban poor in charity and prayer and love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regulars: Regulars are the religious bound by rule. This entry explains their kinds, their privileges, and their law. The soldiers of the cloister: their solemn vows bind the whole life to God alone forevermore in love and service and prayer and praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scala-sancta-: The Scala Sancta is the Holy Stairs of the Lateran. This entry explains its legend, its shrine, and its pilgrims. The stairs of Pilate's praetorium: their worn steps draw the pilgrims in Rome's Lateran in the 1500s' decades of the popes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seekers: The Seekers were the waiters for the true church. This entry examines their doctrine, their leaders, and their end. The sect of the suspended judgment: its patient waiters sought the church in the 1640s' England in the wars of the king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seven-robbers: The Seven Robbers, the repentant thieves of the desert, turned to Christ. This brief entry notes their legend and their cult. A quiet name from the Egyptian sands: their hard penance crowned the desert in the Thebaid's caves in Egypt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sicilian-vesp: The Sicilian Vespers was the rising of 1282. This entry traces its causes, its massacre, and its sequel. The Easter Monday of Palermo: its fateful bells rang the rising in 1282's March in the island of the south in the straits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-fr: The Society of Friends are the Quakers of George Fox. This entry examines their inner light, their meetings, and their history. The people of the silent worship: their silent meetings dotted England in the 1650s' decades in the counties of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-ma: The Society of Mary are the Marist Fathers of Colin. This entry covers their rule, their missions, and their houses. The priests of the Oceania apostolate: their many missions dotted the Pacific in the 1830s' decades in the islands of the ocean.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-desiderius: St. Desiderius was the bishop of Cahors. This entry traces his see, his letters, and his fame. The prelate of the Quercy church: his ancient see crowned Cahors in the 630s' Quercy in the Lot of the valley in the south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gregory-of: St. Gregory of Tours was the historian of the Franks. This long entry examines his History, his see, and his fame. The Herodotus of the Merovingian age: his great History crowned Tours in the 590s' Francia in the west of the kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hilary-of-: St. Hilary of Poitiers was the Athanasius of the West. This long entry examines his Trinity, his exile, and his fame. The doctor of the Gallic church: his great Trinity crowned Poitiers in the 350s' Gaul in the west of the province.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-martin-of-: St. Martin of Tours was the bishop of the cloak. This long entry examines his Marmoutier, his Franks, and his cult. The apostle of the Gallic church: his great see crowned Tours in the 370s' Gaul in the Loire of the river.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-statute-of-pr: The Statute of Provisors was the English anti-papal law. This entry traces its Edward, its Rome, and its effect. The bar of the fourteenth century: its stern clauses crowned Westminster in the 1351 of the Parliament in the hall of the Commons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stedingers: The Stedingers were the peasants of the German marshes. This entry traces their crusade, their defeat, and their story. The heretics of the thirteenth century: their bloody defeat crowned the marshes in the 1234 of the crusade in the Weser.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-surnames-of-f: The surnames are the epithets of the doctors. This entry traces their Angelic, their Seraphic, and their fame. The titles of the great theologians: their proud epithets crowned the schools in the 1200s' universities in the halls of the masters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synodal-exami: Synodal examiners are the testers of candidates. This entry traces their appointment and their duties. The judges of the clerical fitness: their searching tests crowned the candidates in the 1500s' seminaries in the colleges of the truly very old orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-apostolic: The Apostolic Fathers are the first Christians. This very long entry examines their Clement, their Ignatius, and their writings. The witnesses of the apostolic age: their burning letters crowned the churches in the 100s' Asia in the province of the Proconsul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-crosiers: The Crosiers are the canons of the Cross. This entry traces their Liège, their houses, and their rule. The brethren of the holy rood: their red crosses crowned Liège in the 1210s of the crusade in the very old town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-military-: The Military Orders were the armed monks. This very long entry examines their Templars, their Hospitallers, and their history. The swords of the crusades: their stern castles crowned the Levant in the 1100s of the crusade in the old hills.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ten-thous: The Ten Thousand Martyrs are the legend of Ararat. This entry traces their Achatius, their crosses, and their fame. The army of the crucified confessors: their ten thousand crosses crowned Ararat in the 100s of the Hadrian in the legions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-third-orders: The Third Orders are the lay tertiaries. This very long entry examines their Franciscans, their Dominicans, and their rules. The penitents of the world: their holy rules crowned Assisi in the 1220s of the Francis in the very old Porziuncola.
